newsitem.title: USA: CME Taiwan futures set for controversial launch.
newsitem.headline: CME Taiwan futures set for controversial launch.

text.p: The Chicago Mercantile Exchange will launch futures and options on the Dow Jones Taiwan stock index Wednesday night, but competition rather than cooperation has marked this latest global link in the futures industry.

"I think the issue has been one of competition from the Taiwanese point of view, and I think they see and feel, as we do, that there is a lot of interest in trading this product," Rick Kilcollin, CME president-designate, said in an interview.
Almost simultaneously, the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) is launching its own futures contracts based on Morgan Stanley's Taiwan index.
The new contracts will allow investors unprecedented access to futures and options on the Taiwan stock market, the world's sixth largest in dollar terms.
The CME's contracts will begin trade on the GLOBEX after-hours electronic trading system at 1900 CST Wednesday (0100 GMT Thursday), five minutes after SIMEX's launch.
However, both launches have been dampened by rhetoric from Taiwanese regulators, which has included threats to cut off access to stock price data from the Taiwan Stock Exchange.
"They could cut off all the wires, but they'd hurt themselves in so many ways," Merton Miller, a Nobel economics laureate and a CME public director, said in an interview.

The CME's Kilcollin also dismissed the possibility that Taiwan would stop publishing information. He said the most critical information for Dow Jones & Co, which licenses the index and will transmit prices, is individual stock prices.
"It's difficult to imagine that the Taiwan Stock Exchange would stop publishing stock prices," Kilcollin said.

Taiwan's Securities and Exchange Commission Vice-Chairman Hsu Yung-pang told reporters on Wednesday that Taiwan had not authorized local trading of the CME or SIMEX contracts, and he urged investors not to try trading the contracts through "illegal futures brokerages."
Kilcollin said the CME has been working towards getting the CME contracts approved in Taiwan, but he would not speculate when Taiwan might approve the contracts.
"The whole history with them is that things have gone a lot more slowly," he said.

Taiwan has not listed futures and options on its native Taiwan stock index because of delays in opening the country's first futures exchange. The Chicago Board of Trade is helping Taiwan open its first futures exchange.

The CME had planned to launch its contracts in November 1996, but Taiwanese regulators' complaints that the contracts could increase volatility in Taiwan's stock market led the CME to delay the start until January 15.
"There is a feeling (on the part of Taiwan's regulators) that 'By God, it's our market,'" Miller said.
"But its an international world and you can't take that attitude," he added.

The CME decided to list the contracts on January 8 since the exchange did not receive an information-sharing agreement with Taiwan which it had sought in return for postponing the launch date to January 15, the CME said.
Currently, the CME's Dow Jones Taiwan stock index futures and options will compete with SIMEX's Taiwan stock index futures contract for market share.
Kilcollin would not speculate on the amount of business that could be potentially generated from Taiwan stock index futures.
He said the Dow Jones Taiwan stock index, which comprises 117 of the largest and most liquid stocks, rose 35 percent in 1996.
The Pacific Stock Exchange will list options on the Dow Jones Taiwan Stock Index in cooperation with the CME. ((Derivatives desk 312-408-8750;E-mail derivatives@reuters))
